name: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
description: This work systematically evaluates object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs) and proposes a polling-based query method called POPE for more stable and flexible evaluation. The study evaluates representative LVLMs on MSCOCO and also extends evaluation with SEEM-based annotations to A-OKVQA and GQA.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
citeAs: Li, Yifan, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, and Ji-Rong Wen. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355.
rai:dataCollection: The evaluation data are built from existing image datasets. For CHAIR evaluation, the authors randomly sample 2,000 images from the validation set of MSCOCO with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions. For POPE on MSCOCO, they randomly select 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in the annotations and construct 6 questions for each image. POPE constructs triples consisting of an image, multiple object-probing questions, and Yes/No answers. Ground-truth objects are obtained either from human annotations or from automatic segmentation results using SEEM. Negative objects are sampled under Random, Popular, and Adversarial settings.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and annotations from MSCOCO validation set; images from A-OKVQA and GQA annotated using SEEM for automatic segmentation-based POPE. MSCOCO annotations include contained objects and human-labeled captions.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For CHAIR, the study follows settings in Rohrbach et al. (2018) and only considers 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge. For POPE, the authors set the ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects as 1:1 for label balance. They construct polling questions from ground-truth objects and sampled nonexistent objects using Random, Popular, and Adversarial sampling strategies.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For computing CHAIR on MSCOCO, the authors randomly sample 2,000 validation images and only consider 80 MSCOCO objects. For POPE on MSCOCO, they randomly select 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects and construct 6 questions per image. Questions are generated using the template 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?'. For unannotated settings, SEEM is used to segment images and provide object labels for building POPE.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The study uses existing human annotations from MSCOCO for ground-truth objects and captions. For scalable POPE, images from MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA are automatically annotated using SEEM. POPE labels are created by formulating object presence questions with answers 'Yes' for ground-truth objects and 'No' for sampled nonexistent objects.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes differences between annotation-based POPE and SEEM-based POPE, noting that segmentation results from SEEM are finer-grained and may use a label set inconsistent with collected human annotations, which can lead to divergence in evaluation results. The authors also validate consistency between POPE Yes/No responses and objects mentioned in captions.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that object hallucination hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment and may result in unexpected consequences caused by hallucinated objects. It gives autonomous driving as an example, where incorrect understanding of the external environment could lead to wrong decisions and serious safety issues. The authors hope the work can inspire development of more reliable and human-aligned LVLMs.
rai:dataBiases: The paper finds that LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects in visual instruction datasets and objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects in images. It also notes that visual instruction datasets constructed mostly based on MSCOCO share an unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset, which may bias hallucinations toward common objects.
rai:dataLimitations: The work only focuses on object hallucination and does not measure overall LVLM capability. Due to computational limitations, models are evaluated on only part of each dataset validation set, so results may be affected by data distribution. POPE uses a matching-based method to determine whether LVLMs answer 'Yes' or 'No', and models may fail to provide explicit answers containing these words, causing inaccurate evaluation. When combined with automatic segmentation, object labels may be inconsistent with human annotations, leading to divergent results. The study also compares only a small number of LVLMs and excludes some recently released or closed-source models.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset constructions are used for evaluation of object hallucination in LVLMs. CHAIR is used on MSCOCO captions, and POPE is proposed as a binary-question evaluation benchmark under Random, Popular, and Adversarial settings. POPE can also be extended to unannotated datasets with automatic segmentation tools such as SEEM. The paper also uses the resulting evaluations to analyze relationships between hallucination and VQA/image captioning performance.
